content: Recall bias, also known as reporting bias in psychology, is a specific type of systematic bias that arises when a survey respondent's answer to a question is influenced not only by the actual correct answer but also by the respondent's memory. This phenomenon can significantly impact the accuracy of survey results. For instance, consider a hypothetical scenario where J. Simpson is found to have killed his wife, ten years after the conclusion of the criminal trial. Respondents who initially believed in his innocence might be more likely to have forgotten details about the case over time. As a result, they may be more inclined to provide no opinion when surveyed, compared to respondents who believed he was guilty. If this occurs, the survey results could inaccurately reflect a higher proportion of people who believe that Simpson did, in fact, kill his wife. In a related but distinct context, recall bias can also describe situations where a survey respondent deliberately provides an incorrect answer to a question about their personal history, leading to response bias. For example, imagine a researcher conducting a survey among women in Group A, asking whether they have had an abortion, and then conducting the same survey among women in Group B. If the results differ between the two groups, it could be due to women in one group being less likely to have had an abortion. Alternatively, it could be that women in one group who have had abortions are less likely to admit to it. If the latter is true, this would distort the survey results, representing a form of response bias. It is also possible that both factors are at play: women in one group may indeed be less likely to have had abortions, and those who have had abortions may be less likely to disclose it. Either way, the survey statistics would be affected. In experimental sciences, the term reporting bias refers to the tendency to underreport unexpected or undesirable experimental results. Researchers may attribute such results to experimental error while placing greater trust in expected or desirable outcomes, even though these may be subject to the same experimental errors. Over time, this type of reporting bias can create a status quo where multiple investigators independently discover and discard experimental results. Later researchers may justify their own reporting bias by observing that previous experimenters reported different results, even though those earlier experimenters may have also been influenced by a weaker form of reporting bias. Consequently, each instance of reporting bias increases the likelihood of future occurrences, perpetuating the cycle.
